newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's Tyhypko outlines recipe for recovery.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's Tyhypko outlines recipe for recovery.

text.p: The man assigned the task of heaving Ukraine's economy out of its longstanding slump revealed on Thursday his recipe to improve life for the average citizen and ease up the former Soviet republic's investment climate.
"We need an effective economy and unfortunately we don't have that," Serhiy Tyhypko told a news conference.
"We want to build an economy for real people in Ukraine."

The 12-step programme put top government officials, ministers and the central bank governor in charge of areas such as administrative reform, deregulation, taxation and banking reform, privatisation, and investment policies.
"This will take a large amount of work," Tyhypko said of an economy whose first post-Soviet growth was forecast at zero this year and which shrank 10 percent in 1996.

Tyhypko was appointed in April by President Leonid Kuchma, father of Ukraine's first economic reform programme since it won independence in 1991, to replace Viktor Pynzenyk who quit over delays in this year's budget.
The new deputy prime minister, a banker by profession, said the budget would be passed in a week to 10 days, almost six months after Ukrainian law said it should have been.
Ukraine has attracted only $1.4 billion in foreign investment since independence, about 60 percent of the economy is grey and wage arrears are about $2.1 billion.
Tyhypko stressed the need to reduce licensing requirements, remove bureaucratic barriers and slash punitive taxes to allow small- and medium-sized businesses to flourish.
"Deregulation. A new word is appearing in the Ukrainian lexicon," Tyhypko said, adding it was vital to axe investment problems for local and foreign investors.

Several prominent deals with foreign companies including U.S. telecoms giant Motorola have fallen through in recent months amid a cacophony of complaints about incomprehensible and ever-changing rules and demands for bribes.
The draft budget, being passed in concert with nine tax reform laws, forecasts annual inflation of about 25 percent this year against 39.7 percent a year ago.
Without it Ukraine will not get a multi-billion-dollar three-year credit from the International Monetary Fund on which the bulk of its economic programme depends.
